board.headline: DeepMind agents formally verify Signal's code
board.summary: Formal verification means proving mathematically that code does what its specification says. Under AlphaProof Code, human experts work with models to write the security specifications and review every one. Agents running on Gemini Carbon then write the proofs in Lean (a proof language whose checker confirms each step). They generated more than six million lines of proof covering key security properties of the actual Signal protocol implementation, including protection of messages before and after a device is temporarily compromised. The agents flagged about 1% of the work for human review. DeepMind says the effort took four weeks against a historical norm of years. Reintroduced past bugs were correctly proven insecure.
board.why: If this holds up, it moves formal verification from protocol designs to the code that actually ships, which is where real vulnerabilities tend to hide. The claims of "first" and "years" are DeepMind's own. The proofs are only as good as the human-reviewed specifications.

board.headline: Google ships Gemini 4 Hydrogen as its default fast model
board.summary: Hydrogen is Google's fast execution model. It sits alongside the frontier Gemini 4 Carbon and Argon models and replaces Gemini 3.8 Flash across the Gemini app, Search, AI Studio and the API. It costs $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens, flat across a 1-million-token context window. Google says it scores 51 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default setting, against Argon's 50. It also claims Hydrogen more than triples 3.8 Flash on Terminal-Bench 4.1 (57% vs 18.2%) and cuts fabricated claims more than fivefold.
board.why: The fast tier is getting close to last month's frontier at a fraction of the price, and that changes routing decisions in agent pipelines. All figures are Google's.

board.headline: Kremlin says no decision on European seat
board.summary: US envoy Jared Kushner said late on Thursday 12 November, after he and Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in Moscow, that Putin had agreed to include Europe in the Ukraine peace talks. On Friday 13 November the Kremlin said it had not yet agreed. "We cannot conclude this deal without the Europeans being at the table," Kushner said in Dublin, where the envoys briefed Volodymyr Zelensky. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow would decide on "an expanded format" only "once we understand their real intentions". EU leaders were meeting informally in Dublin on Friday, the day after the European Political Community summit, to settle who would speak for the bloc. The talks between Russia and Ukraine are expected to resume next week, the week starting Monday 16 November. Overnight, Russia said it intercepted 1,198 Ukrainian drones over more than 15 regions; four people were killed in Volgograd. Russian strikes hit Odesa, killing at least two people, and set a Kyiv hospital on fire.
board.why: Europe's place at the table is now the main open question in the talks, and Moscow appears to be using it as a bargaining chip while it holds firm on its territorial demands.

sources.label: Irish Presidency of the Council of the EU — EPC meeting page

board.headline: Germany plans €210bn new debt for 2027
board.summary: On the night of Thursday 12 to Friday 13 November, the German Bundestag's budget committee signed off on the 2027 federal budget. It includes just over €210 billion of new borrowing, the second-highest amount in the Federal Republic's history. The figure counts borrowing through the off-budget "special funds" for the military and infrastructure as well as the core budget. New debt makes up about a third of total spending, against just under €400 billion in tax revenue. Only 2021, at the height of the pandemic, was higher, at €215.4 billion. Chancellor Friedrich Merz's proposed cut to the electricity tax did not survive: Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil (SPD) said there was no fiscal room for it, and the SPD said it would have to be paid for with more debt. The committee's sign-off is the last major step before the full Bundestag votes on the budget.
board.why: Germany is Switzerland's largest trading partner. A Berlin borrowing for defence and infrastructure on this scale means more demand for Swiss suppliers, but no relief on energy prices for German industry.

board.headline: UN counts 1,167 killed in Haiti in Q3
board.summary: At least 1,167 people were killed and 459 injured in Haiti between July and September, the UN's integrated office in the country (BINUH) said in a human-rights report published on Thursday 12 November. Gangs were responsible for more than 45% of the incidents and self-defence groups for about 5%. More than half of the documented killings and injuries happened during ground or aerial operations by security forces against gangs, sometimes with drone support from a private military company. Gangs that had been driven out of Bel Air and La Saline earlier this year have returned. The UN Security Council has authorised a Gang Suppression Force, but it is not yet fully deployed.
board.why: the operations against the gangs are now themselves the largest source of casualties, which raises questions about how the authorised international force will be run.

board.headline: Zurich to host EPC summit in April 2027
board.summary: Switzerland will host the next European Political Community (EPC) summit, in Zurich on 15 April 2027, the Federal Council announced after Federal President Guy Parmelin attended the ninth summit in Dublin on Thursday 12 November. In Dublin, Parmelin held bilateral talks with Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda, whose country takes over the EU Council presidency next, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham. He presented Switzerland as a place for "confronting different points of view". The EPC brings the whole continent together, inside and outside the EU, and has met twice a year since Prague in October 2022, alternating between EU and non-EU hosts.
board.why: if the Ukraine talks have moved on by April, a Zurich summit would put Swiss diplomacy, and Swiss security planning, at the centre of Europe's postwar discussions.

board.headline: EU rule change on cross-border jobless pay
board.summary: The EU has told Switzerland that its revised social-security coordination rules (Regulations 883/2004 and 987/2009) are now in force, and the Federal Council will consider "in due course" whether to adopt them. Switzerland says they bring "significant changes" to unemployment insurance for cross-border workers. The point came up at the 29th Swiss–EU Joint Committee on the free-movement agreement in Bern. The Swiss communiqué was published on Wednesday 12 November but dates the meeting to 12 October. The delegations were led by Regula Mader of the State Secretariat for Migration and the Commission's Nicolas von Lingen. The communiqué does not spell out the changes. As the EU adopted it, the revision means that the country where a cross-border worker was last employed, rather than the country where they live, generally becomes responsible for paying their unemployment benefits.
board.why: if Switzerland adopts the rules, the Swiss unemployment fund, not France, Italy or Germany, would pay many cross-border workers when they lose their jobs, a cost that has long been contested in the Bilaterals debate.

board.headline: Microsoft 365 outage hits Outlook and Teams
board.summary: A global outage of Microsoft 365 that began on Thursday 12 November disrupted Outlook, Teams and Copilot in dozens of countries. Microsoft said its fixes "are not taking as expected" and that it was "not aware" of any malicious activity. Downdetector logged reports from 74 countries and territories within about an hour, and nearly 130,000 US reports of Outlook problems. Microsoft said some restarted servers stopped responding again once traffic returned. At 02:54 GMT on Friday it said it was trying other ways to restore service. It is the second disruption to Microsoft 365 this year.

board.headline: Swiss producer prices up 0.9% in October
board.summary: Switzerland's producer and import price index rose 0.9% in October from September, to 101.6 points (December 2025 = 100), the Federal Statistical Office said on Friday 13 November. Prices were also 0.9% higher than in October 2025. The monthly rise came mainly from petroleum products, hydrocarbons, electrical equipment, IT and electronic goods, and machinery.

board.headline: Family leave initiative qualifies for vote
board.summary: The popular initiative for a family leave ("Une société et une économie fortes grâce au congé parental") has formally qualified, the Federal Chancellery said on Thursday 12 November, after it found 111,151 of the 112,529 signatures submitted on 30 September to be valid. The Federal Council and Parliament must now take a position on it before it goes to a national vote.

board.headline: US envoys meet Putin after Abu Dhabi talks
board.summary: US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff arrived in Moscow on Thursday 12 November to meet Vladimir Putin, a day after the first US-mediated direct talks between Russia and Ukraine since February ended in Abu Dhabi with a prisoner-exchange deal but no breakthrough on ending the war. The two days of trilateral talks closed on Wednesday 11 November. Russia's TASS news agency, citing Lieutenant General Alexander Sorin, reported that each side will exchange more than 1,000 prisoners within the next two to three weeks. Positions on territory remain far apart: Russia, which controls about a fifth of Ukraine, wants Kyiv to give up the whole Donbas region, and President Volodymyr Zelensky rejects any cession of land. Ukraine's negotiator David Arakhamia called the talks "hard" and said a solution "before the new year" was possible; Kushner called them "a good first step". After Moscow, the envoys are due to meet Zelensky in Dublin on Friday 13 November, where more than 40 European leaders are meeting today at the European Political Community summit. Russia's chief negotiator Vladimir Medinsky said the Russian side had no contact with the European officials present in Abu Dhabi.
board.why: a prisoner swap of this size is the only concrete result so far, and the next step depends on whether Putin accepts Europeans at the table, which Washington and Kyiv want and Moscow has refused.

board.headline: Israel readies military for possible Iran strike
board.summary: Israel's security cabinet, chaired by caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, ordered the military to step up preparations for a possible attack on Iran, the public broadcaster KAN reported on the evening of Wednesday 11 November. KAN said the directives "could lead it to carry out activities that could trigger a war". They became public after opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, whom President Isaac Herzog asked to form a government after Netanyahu's coalition lost its majority in the October election, told Netanyahu not to use the military "without a direct and immediate threat" until a new government is in place. Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei replied that every base used in an attack, "from West Asia to Europe", would be a target. The reports come while Qatar is trying to broker a US–Iran deal. KAN's report has not been confirmed by the Israeli government.
board.why: a government with no majority would be preparing a possible new war while its likely successor objects, and Iran's threat now explicitly covers bases in Europe.

sources.label: Al Jazeera, 12 Nov 2026 — Iran warns of expanded retaliation as Israel reportedly readies to attack

board.headline: Democrat Colom wins Mississippi Senate seat
board.summary: Democrat Scott Colom defeated Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi, the Associated Press projected on Wednesday 11 November, after more than a week of counting from the 3 November midterm election. Colom, 43, becomes the state's first Black US senator since Reconstruction and the first new Democratic senator Mississippi has elected since 1947. According to DW, the result gives Democrats 55 of the Senate's 100 seats, with Alaska still undecided. Democrats also won the House of Representatives.

sources.label: DW, 12 Nov 2026 — Mississippi Senate race: Democrat Scott Colom wins

board.headline: Spain stages first general strike in 14 years
board.summary: Spain began its first general strike in 14 years at midnight on Wednesday 11 November, a 24-hour walkout over housing costs and purchasing power less than three weeks before the snap election of Sunday 29 November. The two main unions, UGT and CCOO, reported stoppages of around 90% in the car and port sectors in the first hours, according to their own statement relayed by Al Jazeera. Public transport was disrupted, burning-tyre roadblocks went up in Barcelona, and picketers scuffled with police outside Mercamadrid, the capital's main wholesale market. Average rents in Spain have nearly doubled in ten years. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called the election after his minority government failed to pass a housing package. He says the strike is "not against anyone"; business groups call it an election protest, and the conservative Popular Party and Vox have criticised it.
board.why: housing is now the central issue of an election that Al Jazeera says could bring the far right to power, and the strike measures how much pressure the unions can still apply.

board.headline: Stopping statins after 70 passes, with a cost
board.summary: Statins clearly prevent heart attacks in middle-aged people, but whether people over 70 who never had cardiovascular disease should keep taking them has never been tested in a randomised trial. STREAM, sponsored by Inselspital and run mostly through Swiss hospitals and family doctors, randomised 1,880 people aged 70 or older to stop or continue their statin. Sites were in Switzerland, the Netherlands and France, and every participant had at least two chronic conditions. Mean age was 77.5. The main test was non-inferiority: was stopping not meaningfully worse over two years? It passed. Event-free time over two years was 96.5 weeks after stopping versus 98.5 weeks with continuing. The difference of −2.0 weeks fell inside the prespecified −5.2-week margin. But over a median 103 weeks, the composite of non-fatal heart attack, non-fatal ischaemic stroke or death occurred in 12.7% of those who stopped versus 9.2% of those who continued (hazard ratio 1.38, 95% CI 1.05–1.81). The investigators estimate one extra major event or death per 40 people who stop over two years. In June 2026 the safety board recommended that people in the stop arm be told to discuss restarting with their doctor. So the trial met its pre-set test while also showing measurable harm, and commentators disagree about which reading should guide practice. The NEJM full text was not reachable here, so the figures come from HCPLive's report of the paper.
board.why: this is the first real evidence on a decision that millions of older people face, and it comes from Swiss primary care. The authors' own conclusion is "cautious" discontinuation only after shared decision-making, not a general licence to stop.

board.headline: House Republicans shelve Hegseth impeachment
board.summary: The US House voted 211 to 204 on Tuesday 10 November to send Thomas Massie's impeachment resolution against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to the Republican-led Judiciary Committee, which in practice ends the effort in this Congress. Massie, a Republican, had warned that referral would kill the resolution, which accuses Hegseth of waging the Iran war without congressional authorisation. Hegseth called the accusations "slander" and "a farce" at his first Pentagon press conference in months; Donald Trump said the effort had "miserably FAILED". Massie said his colleagues "know it's a sinking ship but committed to stay on board". Democrats take control of both chambers in January, and a new attempt is expected then.

board.headline: US soldier held in UK on Russia spying suspicion
board.summary: British counter-terrorism police arrested a 41-year-old member of the US Army near Gloucester on Tuesday 10 November on suspicion of offences under the National Security Act 2023, in a case the Metropolitan Police say relates to Russia. Officers searched two locations in Gloucestershire. The Met says the investigation was run with US authorities, the US military and the FBI. FBI Director Kash Patel called the espionage allegations of "utmost concern", and the head of US Army Counterintelligence Command described the suspect as a "senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information". The area is home to Britain's signals-intelligence agency GCHQ in nearby Cheltenham and to a NATO rapid-reaction corps headquarters. The man has not been charged.

board.headline: Atoms cooled below 10 picokelvin in orbit
board.summary: A Bose–Einstein condensate (BEC) is a cloud of atoms cooled so far that they share one quantum state and behave like a single wave. In space you can let the cloud float and expand for seconds without it falling, and slower expansion means a lower "equivalent temperature". The previous record, 38 picokelvin (trillionths of a degree above absolute zero) with 2 s of free expansion, used magnetic traps on an atom chip. This team made the condensate aboard the China Space Station in an optical dipole trap, which holds atoms with focused laser light rather than magnetic fields. That design has better optical access and can also trap non-magnetic atoms, but no one had used it to make a quantum gas in microgravity before. Their cloud of 2.0 × 10⁴ atoms reached 9.7 pK (+3.2/−2.7) and expanded freely for 7.0 s. The result rests on the paper's own measurement. Science's news section calls it the coldest temperature yet produced, but no independent group has checked it.
board.why: longer, colder free fall is what atom interferometers need for tests of gravity and the equivalence principle in space. It also shows that laser-based traps, which suit more atomic species, now work in orbit.

board.headline: Cuprate pseudogap marks where electrons pair
board.summary: In copper-oxide ("cuprate") high-temperature superconductors, a partial energy gap called the pseudogap opens well above the temperature at which the material superconducts. For three decades one camp has said it shows electrons already pairing up without yet moving in step. The other camp says it is a competing order, such as charge-density waves (periodic ripples in electron density). The Leiden-led team used local shot-noise spectroscopy on Bi₂Sr₂CaCu₂O₈₊δ. Shot noise is the graininess of an electric current, and it doubles when charge moves in pairs (2e) rather than as single electrons. They find that the pseudogap energy coincides with the onset of pairing, that it varies from place to place, and that it reaches up to 70 meV. The authors say this rules out an origin purely in local order. In their reading, cuprates are limited by phase coherence (getting the pairs to lock in step), not by forming pairs at all.
board.why: if pairs already exist at the pseudogap scale, the way to raise the superconducting temperature is to make those pairs coherent, not to make new ones. That narrows a debate that has shaped materials research for 30 years. The work comes from Dutch and German labs.

board.headline: Iron melts lower at core pressures
board.summary: The temperature of Earth's core is set by where iron melts at enormous pressure, and estimates have disagreed by more than 1,000 K. Carnegie's team squeezed iron in diamond anvil cells and heated it with microsecond current pulses (pulsed Joule heating), spotting melting as a brief temperature plateau. The plateau marks the latent heat being absorbed. More than 300 reproducible runs give a surprisingly shallow melting curve, rising about 6 K per gigapascal and reaching 4,160 ± 80 K at 200 GPa. The team also measured liquid iron's electrical resistivity, 76 μΩ·cm. Extrapolating to core pressures and alloy composition, they infer a relatively cold core–mantle boundary of about 3,430 K and a low heat flow from the outer core of about 9.8 TW. The extrapolation is the uncertain step, and these numbers are the authors' model inference, not direct measurements of the core.
board.why: a cooler core with lower resistivity means ordinary thermal convection could have powered Earth's magnetic field before the solid inner core formed. That bears on the long-running "new core paradox" about how the early magnetic field was sustained. It also implies that the lowest mantle is fully solid today.

board.headline: Ice-age ocean flips took over a century
board.summary: During the last ice age, Greenland repeatedly warmed by many degrees in "Dansgaard–Oeschger" (DO) events. These are usually read as abrupt restarts of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC), the current system that carries heat north toward Europe. Greenland ice cores suggest each warming took only decades, or about ten years. This team used precisely dated cave formations (speleothems) from the Asian monsoon region, whose oxygen isotopes track the same events. Those records show the warmings unfolding over more than a century. Isotope modelling reconciles the two archives. Greenland mostly records a fast change in atmospheric circulation, triggered when sea ice first retreated in the northeastern North Atlantic. The ocean overturning and the hemisphere's heat balance adjusted much more slowly.
board.why: "abrupt" ice-core transitions are often used as benchmarks for how fast the AMOC can switch. This paper says those benchmarks measure the atmosphere's response, not the ocean's. Europe's climate depends on the AMOC, so the distinction matters, although the paper is about natural glacial events, not today's warming.
board.affiliation_label: Xi'an Jiaotong University, British Antarctic Survey +1

board.headline: 3.95-billion-year-old rock found in China
board.summary: Rocks older than 3.9 billion years are so rare that the only accepted examples come from the Acasta Gneiss in Canada. This team reports a 3.95-billion-year-old trondhjemitic gneiss, a light-coloured granite-like rock, from eastern Hebei in the North China Craton. Zircon crystals in it have elevated oxygen-18 (δ¹⁸O about +6.8‰) and positive hafnium-isotope values. Together these suggest the magma came from basalt that had been altered by water near the surface, itself derived from a mantle already depleted during the Hadean, Earth's first eon. Thermodynamic modelling puts its formation at more than 1.6 GPa and 740–820 °C, by low-degree melting of basaltic crust. That requires surface rock to have been buried quickly to mantle depths along a cool path. The authors propose a "transient subduction event", one plate sinking beneath another, rather than continuous plate tectonics. Nature's news coverage treats it as a second window on the period alongside Acasta.
board.why: when plate tectonics began is one of geology's biggest open questions, and a second >3.9-billion-year-old rock body with a high-pressure signature gives that debate a new data point. One sample site is a narrow base, and "transient subduction" is the authors' interpretation.
board.affiliation_label: Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences, Jilin University +1

board.headline: Scythian hair shows 2,800-year-old cannabis use
board.summary: A team led by Bern archaeologist Gino Caspari excavated a monumental Scythian tomb in Tuva, southern Siberia. The Scythians were a horse-riding culture of the Eurasian steppe. The tomb held about 1,000 cannabis seeds, and radiocarbon dating of six of them places the burial in the early 8th century BC. Seeds alone do not prove anyone got high, since hemp was also grown for oil and fibre. The decisive evidence came from preserved human hair. High-resolution mass spectrometry found clear signals matching cannabinol (CBN), a breakdown product of THC, the plant's main psychoactive compound, plus weak signals consistent with THC itself. The Bern release is careful about the limits. The hair cannot say how much was consumed, or whether it was smoked or eaten. The seeds come from wild or feral plants, so they do not show cultivation.
board.why: it pushes direct, in-the-body evidence of psychoactive cannabis use back to at least 2,800 years ago. It also combines plant remains with chemistry from a human body, a method other sites can copy.
board.affiliation_label: University of Bern, Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology +1

board.headline: Pill-tuned gene therapy nearly stops seizures
board.summary: The three adults had temporal-lobe epilepsy caused by scarring of one hippocampus (hippocampal sclerosis). They had been diagnosed 10–25 years earlier and had become resistant to at least two drugs. Surgeons infused an adeno-associated virus (AAV9, a harmless virus used as a gene courier) into the patch of brain where each person's seizures start. The virus carried a gene that makes excitatory neurons produce a designer receptor that responds to clozapine. This approach is called chemogenetics. Two weeks after surgery, patients started low-dose clozapine every eight hours, which switches the receptor on and quiets the targeted neurons. Unlike conventional gene therapy, the dose can be adjusted, or stopped. About two months later, monthly seizures had fallen from 4.5 to 0.5 in two patients and from 4 to 0 in the third, with no serious side effects. This is a three-patient report, published as a correspondence letter rather than a full trial. Clozapine at high doses carries cardiovascular and other risks, and long-term use is unstudied. An outside neurologist quoted by Nature raised both points.
board.why: it is a first human proof that a brain circuit can be gene-modified and then tuned with a pill. If it holds up in larger trials, it could become an option for patients who would otherwise need part of their brain surgically removed.

board.headline: Pelacarsen cuts Lp(a) but not heart events
board.summary: Lipoprotein(a), or Lp(a), is a genetically set cholesterol-carrying particle. Genetic studies strongly link high levels to heart disease, and there is no approved drug for it. Pelacarsen, an antisense oligonucleotide (a short synthetic strand that silences the gene's messenger RNA), is developed by Novartis under licence from Ionis. The trial randomised 8,350 patients with prior heart attack, stroke or peripheral artery disease and Lp(a) of at least 70 mg/dL to monthly injections or placebo. The topline miss was announced in September. The full data show how flat the result was. Lp(a) fell 78.4% at 12 months, yet over a median 4.7 years the primary composite (cardiovascular death, heart attack, stroke or urgent revascularisation) occurred in 12.3% versus 12.1% (HR 1.02, 95% CI 0.90–1.15). The result was the same in patients with the highest Lp(a). Flu-like and injection-site reactions were far more common on the drug, 20.6% versus 7.5% stopped treatment because of side effects, and 19 patients on pelacarsen had adjudicated anaphylaxis versus none on placebo.
board.why: it is a sharp reminder that lowering a risk marker does not guarantee fewer events. It is a major setback for Basel-based Novartis's cardiovascular pipeline, and the question now passes to other Lp(a) drugs still in outcome trials.

board.heading: Why it matters
board.title: The marker is not the outcome
paras: Two of this week's cardiology results make the same point from different directions. Pelacarsen removed 78% of a genetically validated risk particle and prevented no heart attacks. In STREAM, stopping a drug passed a pre-set non-inferiority test while event rates still rose by a hazard ratio of 1.38. Both say to judge treatments by what happens to patients, not by what happens to a number on a lab report.

"Abrupt" depends on the recorder. The Dansgaard–Oeschger study and the pseudogap paper both resolve old debates by changing the measuring instrument. Cave records separate the atmosphere's fast response from the ocean's slow one. Shot noise counts the charge of the current carriers directly instead of inferring pairing from an energy gap. In both cases the long-standing "fact" was partly a feature of the instrument.

board.headline: Anthropic ships Claude Fable and Mythos 5.2
board.summary: Fable and Mythos are the same underlying model. Fable carries cybersecurity and biology safeguards and is open to all users, while Mythos goes to vetted organisations through Anthropic's Cyber and Life Sciences Verification Programs. The new versions cost $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, down from $10 input, and generate output up to 30% faster than 5.1. A "fast mode" up to 2.5× faster costs double. On Anthropic's own benchmarks, Fable 5.2 at High effort scores 45.3% on FrontierCode 2.0 (whether maintainers would merge its code changes), level with Opus 5.5's best for about half the cost per task. At Xhigh effort it reaches 49.1%, against 42.8% for GPT-6 Astra. On RoboDojo Sim (control of a simulated two-arm robot, run internally) it scores 64.9% against 29.8% for GPT-6 Astra. On Anthropic's internal CVE Rediscovery test (re-finding 1,829 published vulnerabilities from pre-fix code), Mythos 5.2 found 14.4% more than Mythos 5.1. Anthropic's showcase claims include a team of about 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents formalising Fermat's Last Theorem in the Lean proof language in 30 hours, against 11 days for its earlier attempt, and work on two open problems about black holes in holographic (gravity-to-quantum) physics. Anthropic says high-stakes misalignment risk "remains low". It also writes, as quoted by TechCrunch, that both models "voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models," and that this limits how well tests predict real-world behaviour.
board.why: The price cut and the "same quality as Opus 5.5 for less money" claims change cost decisions for heavy agentic coding users. Every benchmark here is the vendor's own, several were run internally, and the physics and formalisation claims have not been independently verified. The rise in evaluation awareness is the safety detail most worth watching: it weakens the tests that the low-risk verdict rests on.
